utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before an opportunity will be given to the Prosecution to call its witness in its re-opened case, I'd first like to put something on the record. On the 27th of May, 2010, the Trial Chamber instructed the Prosecution and the Victims and Witness Section informally that both Witness 177 and Witness 178 should be present on the Tribunal premises on Thursday morning - that is, tomorrow morning - and are to be kept separate during the day. It is in the same context, and reasons will be formally put on the record later, that we'll hear the evidence of the witnesses today and tomorrow, in private session, which doesn't mean that that evidence will be kept confidential, but for those two days it will. The reasons for that will be put in detail on the record soon. The Chamber verified that the witness who will testify today, he did not ask for any protective measures. So it's a -- as matters stand now, it is a temporary measure. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, at this point, just simply because there has been no Rule 79 or 75 basis for this, we just want to preserve our objection to proceeding in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. We'll put on the record in full detail in open session what the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I just preserve my objection at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Same here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are slightly concerned because there has been so much publicity about this matter as the Court knows and the Court has referred to in earlier proceedings in Croatia and elsewhere. And this will be the first public opportunity of that evidence to be properly heard, and so we are concerned with the measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. And as may be clear to the parties it is not the intention of this Trial Chamber to keep this confidential. It should be part of the public record. It's a -- as matters stand now a temporary measure for which the reasons will be given in detail, and it's clear that all parties reserve their positions in relation to this measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything from the Prosecution side in relation to this? Then we move into private session. And we'll most likely stay in private session for the two days to come.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution would like to call witness 176, Mr. Jozo Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good, Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, you're required to make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bilobrk. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, the Chamber understands that you did not seek any -- apparently you do not hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, actually. I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is informed that you're not seeking any protective measures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, nevertheless, the Chamber decided, not because you're seeking protective measures, that your testimony will be heard in private session. That is, that it is no secret that you're testifying here, but the content of your testimony is not to be disclosed to the outside world. And most likely, this is a temporary measure only, which is related to the integrity of the proceedings rather than anything else. Just for you to know, that, at this moment that no one will hear your testimony. Is that clear? If you have any questions in relation to that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you may ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no questions, I understand fully what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you will first be examined by Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hedaraly, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Jozo Bilobrk. I was born on the 13th of September, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I'm a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What was your occupation in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Before coming here to testify today, did you seek any advice from anyone regarding your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Not about the case or my testimony but about the arrival in The Hague. But -- about my coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I talked to a judge at the county court. But not about the case. I spoke to him about the arrival at the The Hague and -- and possibly if somebody wanted to talk to me before I entered the court, how I should talk to them, and how I should react to such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What did this judge tell you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: He asked me if I had been interviewed by those who were supposed to receive those interviews, who requested those interviews, if -- officially. I said yes. And then he told me that his recommendation would be not to talk to anybody again before I entered court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court why you sought this advice from this judge?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Because I remember that during the investigation there was a lot of pressure, letters were written to replace my statements, although I never provided those statements. I thought that somebody might want to get in touch with me again, and in order to avoid doing something wrong or feeling uncomfortable, I got in touch with that judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Since you arrived in The Hague, did you meet with any of the parties?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I only met with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you discuss with the OTP any of the substance of your expected testimony today?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: The gentleman from the Prosecution suggested that I should be prepared for the trial. We started going over the interview that I had already provided to them, and when I realized that they wanted to discuss the statement that I'd already had, I said that I would retain the right not to say anything else, if there, indeed, was that right, and if there is anything else that they wanted to ask me, that they were welcome to do so here today in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was that the end of your interview with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, I requested from the Prosecution an official translation of the interview that the OTP had conducted with me, because I had not had that official translation. Since I don't speak the English language, and I was provided only with the Defence's version of the interview translated into Croatian, and I could not check whether the Defence's translation tallied with what was in the original, that's why I requested from the Prosecution to provide me with the official translation of my statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to clarify: You requested the English translation of your statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. What I requested was a translation into Croatian. I provided a statement to the OTP, and when I was interviewed by the OTP, I signed the statement in English, which means that I myself could not read the statement myself. There was no statement in -- in Croatian that I could sign -- sign after reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke. You requested a Croatian translation of your statement to the Prosecution, right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Croatian. Croatian. Croatian translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you request any other of the statements that you had made?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. I also requested the statement that I provided to the county court in Zagreb. I only had one opportunity to see it, and that's -- that's why I wanted to have another look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to move to August 1995 and your -- and your role in and around Knin. Can you tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just raise a matter at this stage, and I apologise to my learned friend. It's just a procedural matter. The Court will recall that a 92 ter filing was made by the Defence in respect of interviews with this witness. That was served on the parties and the Court, and a document was filed by the Prosecution not objecting to that becoming a 92 ter exhibit. It occurs to me, because that contains a great deal of background and information from the witness and was taken in his own language, that, in accordance with the previous procedures that we've adopted during this trial, that it would be appropriate for that to be made an exhibit at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a statement taken by the Defence, that they wish to tender into evidence. The Prosecution is calling this witness viva voce. It will put the questions to the witness that it feels is appropriate to get the evidence in front of the Chamber, and then if the Cermak Defence wants to tender its statement under Rule 92 ter as it has suggested it would do, if they then meet the requirements of the rule, then as the Prosecution stated, at that time, it will have no objection. But at this time it is premature. This is the Prosecution's examination and it should not be limited or constrained to put into evidence a statement taken by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to put into evidence, I do not know what Mr. -- it may be very practical to deal with certain matters which are not are in dispute and if they are written down in that statement. Another way of dealing with that is to have it marked for identification for the time being, so that reference can be made to it and that it's at least part of the record. Although not yet admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My thorough Case Manager has ever reminded me that, in fact, Your Honour introduced the statements during the Prosecution case as a way of dealing with this procedurally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember that we once had, instead of cross-examination we had a 92 ter statement which served as a cross-examination. It was one occasion. That was a French witness. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was -- there is also a distinction when the Prosecution -- it did happen in the past, but when the Prosecution also tendered 92 ter statement and then, of course, it would make sense if there is any contradiction in those statements to have that resolved before. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I see that there is a bit of a differences in that we find ourselves in a very special situation. Mr. Hedaraly, if I could urge you to, to the extent - and you certainly have looked at all the statements quite carefully, I take it - that we don't waste time by not referring to a document on undisputed matters or to read from it or to refer to it in any other way. But I do understand that you're not the one who is seeking that document to be admitted into evidence. Let's try to take the practical approach, while, at the same time, fully observing the different positions of the parties. If I could invite you to do that, then I'll let you go. I also want to inform the parties that we'd like, on the basis of the estimates given, it should be possible to conclude the testimony of Mr. Bilobrk today. Two hours Prosecution; one hour for one of the Defence teams; one session for another Defence team. That should do. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please describe briefly what your role was in and around Knin in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: From the police administration of Split -- or, rather, Split and Dalmatia county, I was referred to the police administration of Zadar to assist them in the territory of the police station in Knin, with regard to the humane disposal of the dead bodies that were found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what would be the general procedure for that? What would be -- what would do you on a -- on a given day, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: When we receive information that a dead body is found in an area, I and my colleagues would -- will go there with members of the civilian protection and pyrotechnicians. We carry out our part of the job which is taking photos of the dead body, making a video-clip of the dead body, the inspection of the clothes, the making record of any artifacts that are found by the body, personal artifacts and personal documents, or anything else that might help us identify such a dead body. Taking finger-prints, if possible, and then when that part of the job is finished, members of the civilian protection, or, rather, before the photos and video-clips are taken, the members of the civilian protection put a number on the body, and once our job was done, that dead body was put in a bag and was transferred for burial at the city cemetery of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did ever conduct an on-site investigation when you collected any of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to talk about the removal of the bodies on the 27th of August, which included the removal of the bodies that were found in Grubori. And I first want to focus on your recollection of what happened as you sit here today, and then we can go through some documents, if that assists your memory. First of all, on the 27th of August, who provided you the information regarding the bodies to be collected that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Before I answer that, I would like to say that yesterday you asked me about what I remembered. I told you that I don't -- no longer had -- have recollections. I have knowledge because Mr. Cermak's Defence showed me all those documents. So I can no longer speak from recollection. I can speak about the things that I know now. That have I full knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What I want to do is I'll ask you -- I'll ask you some questions and if you don't -- you answer on the basis of your knowledge, if that knowledge is based on the documents you were showed, you can say so, and if that knowledge is based on something else, we'll explore that. Just listen to my questions and answer them as we go along, and if you want to seek any clarification as to my question, you should feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So let me ask you again: Who provided you the information regarding the bodies to be collected that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We received information at the operations duty center of the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And at that time was any information given to you about the bodies that you had to collect? For example, the circumstance in which they were -- they were killed, how the bodies were found, or any of that sort of information?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We received information that in the hamlet of Grubori there were five or six dead bodies of the people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you given any additional information about these five or six bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. Before we arrived in the hamlet, we didn't know anything. Once we saw the bodies, we -- we knew more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at some point, did you meet with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, I met General Cermak at Plavno. It's on the local road nearby a bridge, a little bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, what is -- what is the basis for -- let me repeat my question. Now your answer that you met him at Plavno, is that based on your recollection, or is it based on documents that were shown to you by the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: It's based on the documentation. We went to the field daily and we set off in front of the police station. I gave my statement to the OTP, and I stated that the meeting took place in front of the police station. But, on that day, I wasn't able to review the documentation showing what I was doing on that day, because there was another field mission. And once I had given it a thought and reviewed the documents, I concluded that it was physically impossible for us meet in front of the police station at Knin. I know that we were waiting for someone at Plavno and that we met someone there, so it is there that we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Other than the fact that you were shown documents by the Cermak Defence that, as you said, led to you conclude that that's where the meeting took place, do you have any independent recollection of where that meeting took place, yourself, from your memory, can you picture it, or is it solely based on the documents you were shown?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. Once I was shown the documents that show what you did at the time, of course, after 15 years you don't remember all the details. But having seen the documents, regardless of the Defence or anybody else, I remembered meeting General Cermak at Plavno. And I also remember how we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, you're saying that when you saw these documents, that triggered your memory that you met him in Plavno, because earlier you said that that was a logical conclusion that you've derived from the documents. I'm just trying to understand which one it is. Was it your memory now that you remember meeting him in Plavno, or is it just a conclusion that you are deriving from the documents?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I remember us meeting at Plavno after I had reviewed the documents. So this is not a conclusion; it is not a conjecture. The documents refreshed my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me briefly go through some of these documents that you were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's start with 65 ter 2D00-860, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bilobrk, that was -- do you remember that as being one of the documents that were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't know if it's the very document. But this is one of the documents - as far as I can tell from the handwriting, which is mine - that I filled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to the third page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is one of the documents that shows that, on the 27th of August, you also collected a body in Strmica and in Plavno, in addition to the ones in Grubori; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It follows from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There's also a 65 ter 2D00-62?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we make the previous document an exhibit at this stage, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's an attachment to the 92 ter statement, so there's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- but you'd like to have it in evidence now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it assists the Court, because if we refer to it, we then have a live exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, since it was an attachment to the -- that it's the Defence which now that tenders this document, although at a bit of an unusual moment. Please proceed -- Mr. Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D2042, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2042 is admitted into evidence. It will be a public document; although, the content should remain confidential until -- as long as the confidentiality of this hearing has not been lifted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can then go to 65 ter 2D862.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which are the various -- you will see are the various forms that were filled out in that time-period. Do you remember reviewing these documents as well? They were also shown to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I see in the original 289, whereas in the English translation I see 299. I further see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There was only a portion translated by the Defence for the relevant day. The originals included the whole series for a period of five or six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this is not a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's a partial translation of the B/C/S documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see in the original on the first line reference to what seems -- looks very much as civilian, whereas I find in the English, soldier. Now I could make -- I could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see different numbers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There are a number of these forms, one per page, and the original spans, I think, 20 or 25 pages. Only a portion of these pages were translated, so the first page that we see in the English does not correspond to the first page in the B/C/S right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Just for me to know that usually we see an English version and a B/C/S version of the same document. Here, apparently, let's then forget about the English translation of this B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it doesn't correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think if we go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- yes, now we have -- yes, now I see the numbers are corresponding. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you see that is one of the bodies that was collected on the 27th of August in Strmica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We will see the first of the bodies that was collected from Grubori; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, we'll see a second body collected in Grubori. Can you confirm that that's the case?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we turn the page again, we'll have the third victim from Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we again turn the page, we'll have the fourth Grubori victim.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the next page will the fifth and last victim you collected in Grubori that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that's -- yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, we will see the last body you collected on the 27th of August in Plavno.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So these documents were also shown to you in your interview with the Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And these documents also show that, on that day, you collected bodies not only in Grubori but also in Strmica and in Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have 2D00 -- we can have this one as a -- if Mr. Kay wants to tender it, we won't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number of this series of documents would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit D2043 thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2043 is admitted into evidence. And as far as the public character of it, the same applies, as I said before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now another document that was shown to you was 65 ter 2D00-859. And that was a document generally discussing the -- the deployment of police officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Could you please show me the second page, if there is one, so I can see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: This is a document that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, this document doesn't discuss anything about what happened in Plavno that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If my learned friend wants to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, the witness said, "Can I look at page 2 so that I have a look at the whole of the document," it's a five-page document, but I just want to verify that the witness is happy with having seen two pages and not the whole of the document. Mr. Bilobrk, you are satisfied that this is the document you saw, even if it contains more pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see all of the pages of this document too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a bit ambiguous, Mr. Hedaraly, whether he wanted to see just the second page or the whole of the document. This page 3 is now on your screen. Perhaps we move on to page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And page 5 in the English, but there are only four pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I read it. I've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2044. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2044 is admitted into evidence. The same applies, as far as the public character is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Another document you were shown was 65 ter 2D00-861. And if we go to the third page of this document in the original - it's the correct page in the English - now that document, again, shows that on the 27th of August, in addition to the bodies in Grubori, you collected a body in Strmica and in Plavno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this may be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be Exhibit D2045. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Same condition as far as the public character is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You were also shown 65 ter 2D00-863. And if we move through these documents one page at a time, can you confirm that this is the information regarding the body that was collected in Plavno, in addition to the ones in Grubori, on the 27th of August.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. By the identification number that we put on the corpse this is 542, Stevan Vidovic. If you could turn to page 1, because I can't really remember all of it. Yes, in the village of Plavno, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this one can be made an exhibit I suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D2046. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2046 is admitted into evidence. Same applies as to the public character. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you were also shown 65 ter 1414, which, this time, is the identification form of the victim of the body that you collected in Strmica. You'll see the name and the number come up as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We can move through the pages slowly so the witness has the time to look at them. If we can move to the next page, if there is -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember that document also being shown to you about the body that you collected in Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: This is a document that was shown to me, but I cannot remember by the number. I would have to look at the identification form, so only then I would be able to tell where the body was found. Merely by looking at the body, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But you remember being shown that -- that picture?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I have that as an exhibit as well, on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit D2047. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2047 is admitted into evidence. Same applies as to the public character.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now the last contemporaneous document that was shown to you was D57, which is the log-book of the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 59 of the English and page 61 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember being shown that document, Mr. Bilobrk?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I thought that was page 61 of the original. Is that ... If we can go one page before, please; entry number 193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hedaraly was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now you were shown the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not 193.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you were shown -- one of the entries you were shown was entry 193, where this is a verbal report that information had been received that in Plavno village, Grubori hamlet, on 25 August, two male bodies were found. And then in the next column, it says that it was agreed with Chief Cedo Romanic that an on-site investigation would be conducted in the morning of 27 August and that civilian protection went to the scene at 1100 on 27 August and removed the bodies. And you were also shown entry number 198, which is two pages later in the English. And here there's a report of a decomposing body in Strmica village, and it states that civilian protection is informed that Jukic sent his officers to remove the bodies at 1100, and that seems to be also on the 27th of August. So you were shown these two entries as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us based -- and these were the contemporaneous documents from the time they were shown to you. Now, can you tell us, looking at this, what -- what triggered your memory that your meeting with General Cermak was in Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: In the log-book of events on these two pages that contain the reports on bodies at Plavno and Grubori, we received reports at 1100 hours at the operational duty center of the Knin police station. That's where we received the report. And the duty officer mentioned that. He -- he states that both entries were received at 1100. Because he always assigns a time to every entry. If there had been other bodies elsewhere of which we had knowledge at the same time, we would have had five such entries, all at the same time, all saying 1100 hours. So we were sent off to Plavno. Ours first field mission was to Strmica. We assigned numbers to the dead bodies in the sequence that we processed them during the sanitation. The first body would be assigned a smaller number, and that's how we would proceed. After processing the body, I remember that, at a distance of about 30 kilometres, because that's a distance -- that's a distance to Strmica. So we took some time to get there and return to Plavno. These documents refreshed my memory after 15 years, because that's a long time for anybody to remember some things without reviewing documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand. And I also understand that these documents show that on that day you also went to Strmica to collect a body. I'm not -- I'm not questioning that. I'm simply ask you what refreshed your memory that the meeting with General Cermak took place in Plavno, based on the fact that you collected a body in Strmica and also in Grubori that day. If -- if there -- if both instructions were given to you at 1100 in Knin, isn't it possible that that meeting took place outside the Knin police station before you went off to Strmica or to Plavno, or wherever else?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. These documents jogged my memory. When we left for Plavno, a column of vehicles was waiting on the road, and we joined the people from the civil protection who took to us Plavno because we didn't know the area. And we joined their column of vehicles. I'm certain that that's where the meeting with General Cermak took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's talk about this meeting with General Cermak. So when you arrived there, who was General Cermak with?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: General Cermak was with a group of people, and that group also involved soldiers, members of special police. There was some 15 people perhaps all together. There were also journalists. Some 15 to 20 people all together with their -- me and my colleague joined them. Four members of civil protection also joined them, and I believe that there were two or three explosives experts who also joined the group, which pushed the number to approximately 25 to 30 people. I didn't count heads. But, in any case, the group that was there, in the village of Plavno where we joined the column, General Cermak was there with the -- that group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what is the first thing you remember about this encounter? Did you approach this group, or did this group approach you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We joined the group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you joined the entire group of people?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did you hear from the group?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We joined the conversation. At one point, a person in the group mentioned the fact that weapons were left. They had all -- already been talking before our arrival. I don't know what they were discussing. In any case, a couple minutes after we joined them, somebody mentioned weapons and the fact that weapons were left. And when I heard that some weapons had been left, I reacted. I didn't know, first of all, what we were waiting for, who we were waiting for. We were told that we should be there until somebody came, but I didn't know who -- I didn't know what, I didn't know how many. In any case, what I knew was that there was some bodies in the village of Grubori and that we were supposed to deal with those. And when that person, that somebody mentioned weapons that were left --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What do you mean by [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just -- I'm sorry to do this. But it is for good reason that the -- I have information that the translation from 24:19 down to the end of that answer in the tense that is being used is -- is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you are going to clarify that, Mr. Hedaraly, apparently it struck you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And not being a specialist, but I've just been given information that the sense of what has been said is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that Mr. Hedaraly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wants to seek clarification. Perhaps you do it by going through the answer and see in what respect it is not correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, your answer was translated to us -- was interpreted to us as you heard that weapons were left, that you heard that weapons were left. Several times you said that in the -- in the past tense. Can you tell us what is it that you heard?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That weapons should be left. That the first thing that should be done was to leave weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And was that said loudly or softly?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Some people were talking about that behind my back. Nobody spoke directly to me. It was just what people were saying. I don't know who said it to whom. I didn't pay too much attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was the entire group together at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: When we're talking about a group of people, such a group of people could be the group that are sitting here in the courtroom. We are a group of people. And the same thing was true of Plavno. Not everybody was standing close together. They were scattered in smaller groups, two or three people would be talking, standing there and talking to each other, but, in any case, they all formed a large group of people that belong together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you tell who from this group of people made that suggestions [sic], that weapons should be placed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, that was not the word that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, actually, that weapons should be left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- as a matter of fact, I wanted to seek clarification of that. I refrained from it but since it now becomes in dispute. Weapons should be left suggests that there were weapons, would then -- should be left is that they should remain where they were. Was that it. Or was it that people had seen weapons and that they wanted to put those weapons in the same position where they had found them. What was the gist of the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday I received the translation into Croatian of the statement that I provided to the OTP. And in that statement, as I read it, I read the statement, and the verb there is to place weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, I thought that there was some ambiguity. Whatever you read yesterday and how it was translated, we might come to that at a later stage. What I would like to know is what you just testified. Weapons should be left, is that that they were still in the position where they were found or that they had to be put again in the position where they had been found? Or any other interpretation, such as putting them in a place where they had not been found. What was the gist of what you heard saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I rewind to that time, that should have concerned leaving weapons in the vehicles, which meant that we were not supposed to enter the village with long-barrelled rifles. We as policemen all had long-barrelled rifles, but we left them in the vehicles. There was still people living there. And on reflection I interpreted that as leaving weapons behind in order to avoid scaring those who were still living in the village. But the way I saw it and the way I interpreted what I heard was leaving our weapons behind in the vehicles instead of carrying them with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So let me understand. You heard weapons should be left, and you understood that to mean that weapons should be left in the cars before going to collect the bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how did you react when you heard that being said?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: My first -- my initial reaction was to think that we shouldn't be leaving weapons behind. If there was anybody who should have left weapons behind, they could have done it without me, without me knowing about it. So if anybody had any intentions, I was not aware of any such intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You didn't interpret the fact that bodies should be -- that weapons should be left as meaning that weapons should be left next to the bodies in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, according to my initial reaction, it turns out that way, that somebody should have left weapons by the dead bodies in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, what was your reaction when you heard it? Was it that weapons should be left in the car, or that weapons should be left next to the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, no. My reaction to that was -- actually, my first reaction, the way I understood it at first was that weapons should be left or placed by the bodies. Nobody actually explicitly mentioned that, but when I heard the words, I remember that that was my initial reaction. That's the way I reacted initially. That was my first train of thoughts when I heard somebody talking about weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So when you said a few minutes ago: My first -- my initial reaction was to think that we shouldn't be leaving weapons behind, if there was anybody who should have left weapons behind, they could have done it without me, without me know about it. That, you meant, that that was leaving weapons behind, your first reaction was to understand that as leaving the weapons next to the bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you said earlier that that was part of a -- what you overheard in a conversation. Was it mentioned more than once, was it a discussion among people? What was the context of that suggestion being made?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That was being said or talked about by some persons within that group of people that we joined. And that was said behind my back. I only heard the words. I turned around and I said what I meant. I addressed those words at that little group, and that's how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And who was in that group at that point? Was everyone still in the group? The journalists, the special police members, General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He didn't say everyone was still in a group earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking the question. Who was in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was in the group at that point, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The question was, was everyone still in the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question would have been [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Hedaraly, and the second one was suggestive. Yes, Mr. Bilobrk, would you answer the question, who was still in that group at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cermak was there. There were journalists. At that moment Mr. Cermak was talking to the journalists. And I was looking at him. I saw him when I joined the group. He was amidst a conversation with the journalists. I don't know what they talked about and at that point I herd heard those words about leaving weapons behind, and I offered my comment to those words at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: From where you were standing, could Mr. Cermak have heard the comment that was made?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Cermak could hear those words or not. Perhaps he could. I don't know what his state of health is, whether he has a good sense of hearing. I believe that if he had heard, that he would have reacted in the same way I did, if those words referred to placing weapons by the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And why do you think he would have reacted, if he had heard that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I think at that time I -- I perceived Mr. Cermak as a high state official. He was with the journalists, and I don't think he would have allowed something like that to happen in front of the journalists, in front of a group of 30 people without intervening -- intervening, without offering a comment -- a comment of some sorts, without reacting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I may have missed it. But I'd like to know exactly what your comment was. You heard something about weapons to be left. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will probably not be able to quote my words exactly. However, my first instinctive reaction was that there would be no leaving weapons behind, if that meant leaving weapons behind or placing them by the dead bodies, and if somebody had intended to do that, they could have done it before my arrival, without me know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your response was that you opposed to the suggestion of what you'd heard, and you had understood the words spoken behind your back as a suggestion to put weapons next to the bodies. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you understood me properly. However, when I answered the question about leaving weapons, I meant that if leaving weapons behind referred to leaving weapons behind the dead bodies, possibly, because in that group nobody ever mentioned or used the words "dead bodies." The only words used were about leaving weapons behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the "ifs" and "ands," we should get rid of that. What we are interested to hear is what was said behind your back and what your comment was, and not if this was meant, then my spontaneous reaction would have been ... what I'm interested in, in what you said. Now you say you cannot literally quote that, but I do understand that your comment was opposing to what you heard being suggested. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we may have misunderstood each other. When I said "if," that "if" referred to the words that I uttered towards that group of people that I turned to. Not my words in answering the judge's questions. When I heard a reference being made to leaving weapons behind, I turned towards that group of people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did you then say? What was the gist of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turned around. I turned towards that group of people and I said, If they meant leaving weapons by the dead bodies, they could have done it before I arrived, without me knowing about it. They should have done it before unbeknownst to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened is you hear someone saying, Should we put weapons next to the bodies. Then you turn around, and you say, If you mean to put -- well, let me -- [Overlapping speakers] start over again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You heard someone saying leaving weapons. You turn around. You address those who were speaking and say, If you mean, or if you are suggesting that we should put weapons next to the bodies, then you should have done that before and without my knowledge, which implicitly means that you were opposed against putting weapons at that moment next to the bodies. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that would be the gist of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did they then say, in response to what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was it. There was no further reference made to weapons, and I did not speak to any person. I spoke to the group. And after my words, there were no further references to weapons or leaving weapons behind. The discussion stopped there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also no one said, No, that's not at all what we have in mind. We were talking about leaving our weapons in the car, and -- so no one responded at all to what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no comments proffered. I don't even know whether they paid any attention to my words. When I turned around towards them, I did not hear anybody commenting in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: How far was General Cermak from you when that suggestion was made?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: 4, 5, or 6 metres. I apologise, the distance would be approximately as the distance from me and this column in the middle of the courtroom. 4, 5, 6 metres, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I disagree that it is approximately 5 and a half, 6 metres. A little bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have an opportunity during the break to do it the usual way, big steps. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you turned around and -- and told the group that if what they meant was to leave weapons next to the bodies, they should have done it before you came, did you say that in an angry manner?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. It was a statement more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 7648. Now, in February, you were -- you gave a statement to the county court in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you were cautioned that you had an obligation to tell the truth and that giving a false statement was a criminal act; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also sign a record of the interview?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you signed it, you were satisfied that it accurately reflected what you had said?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to page 5 of the English; page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page in English it says -- well, you say, because it's your statement that you signed: "Furthermore, I believe that General Cermak definitely could have heard when someone from that group of ten-20 soldiers, who had approached me in front of the Knin PU building said that weapons ought to be placed next to the ... bodies. He did not react to that statement at all." Now, I understand that you -- today you are saying that that meeting did not take place in front of the Knin building, based on documents that were shown to you which triggered your memory. But can you explain the difference a few months ago when you said you definitely -- that General Cermak definitely could have heard when that suggestion was made and today?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, there's no difference, actually. Your questions here today are much more detailed than the questions put to me down there. He could hear. He could hear the remark. Whether he did or not, I don't know. You should ask Mr. Cermak that. You should ask him whether he heard anything of the sort. I cannot speculate about stories and about things that Mr. Cermak could or couldn't hear. You could perhaps ask Mr. Cermak whether he did hear those words and how far he was. If he was concentrated and if he was following what was going on in that group, the conversation in the group, then, yes, he could hear the words said by that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not speculate on who was focussed or not. Let's limit ourselves to what distance was, what circumstances were, and then avoid, He may have been thinking about the weather at that moment, which may have -- diverted his attention. That's not for speculation. At the time, you said, He definitely could have heard, which I understand to be that to the extent you were aware of the circumstances such as distance, level of noise, that you would definitely think that he could have heard it, whether he did is a different matter, and that you still stand to that. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understood me very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we move two pages prior in the English and one page prior in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you're relating this -- what happened then to the judge in Zagreb, towards the middle of the page in the English, when you said: "When I heard that, I said that I was not going to place any weapons and that I do not consent to this and that if they wanted to do this, they should have done it earlier so that I wouldn't know about it. I can't remember now who of those people said this. However, I reacted to this immediately. I did not know General Cermak earlier, and I assume that he approached me with that group of soldiers ..." I want to focus on the "I did not know General Cermak earlier." Now, today, at page 30, line 16, when I asked you why you thought he would have reacted, if he had heard that suggestion, you said: "I perceived Mr. Cermak as a high state official at that time." So I'm just trying to clarify, did you know Mr. Cermak, who he was at that time, or you just perceived him to be a high state official based on what you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, we had never met in person. But I recognised him because I knew him from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did you know about him from the media?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I didn't follow the media very closely, but whenever General Cermak was mentioned, there would be a picture of him or he would give a statement or something like that, and that's why I knew what General Cermak looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. And, Mr. Hedaraly, may I take it that you will stay within the time-limits you -- of your estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour. I may be a little over, but I definitely will done in the next session. Hopefully in the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The scheduling is that we try to finish the testimony of Mr. Bilobrk in two hours. Two hours is two hours and is not close to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but as you know those are estimates and sometimes it's hard to keep within those estimates. I am trying to do my best. I'm simply indicating that there is a possibility that I may go over the two hours, and if that is the case, then I will ask the Court's indulgence. I can't give you a specific time right now, I'm hoping that I will be done within 45 minutes or an hour after we come back from the break, but I will try very hard to finish within half an hour, within the two hours that we had estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, we still have your statement to the -- to the judge in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. You may proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We still have in front of us on the screen your statement to the county court in Zagreb. And there you say on the second page, third page in the English: "General Cermak came then, surrounded by a group of people who were wearing Croatian military uniforms and were armed, and there were also a lot of journalists present. When that group stopped, General Cermak and the group of soldiers around him approached me, and I heard them talking among themselves, and that someone had said that weapons ought to be placed next to the dead bodies." And then we discussed the remaining of that portion. Now, what you said today is a little different. Here you say that General Cermak and the group of soldiers approach you and that's when you heard that comment being made; and today you suggested that that actually came from behind you and General Cermak was talking to journalists. Can you clarify for us what exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I only have half the text on the screen. Could I see more? In this section of the statement, a word or two were left out. I said to the county court that in my opinion, the weapons should have been placed next to the dead bodies. Could you please continue? Ask me another question, so I can reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you the same question again. That when that suggestion or that comment was made in this statement to the county court, you said that General Cermak came and that the -- General Cermak and the group of soldiers around him approached you when you heard them talking amongst themselves; whereas, today, you said that that comment came from behind you when General Cermak was in front of you with journalists. I'm asking you to clarify for us which one it is or what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: This statement was given to the county court without my previous review of any documentation. The interview that I gave to you about meeting General Cermak in Knin is mentioned here also. Because, as I said, I didn't have a chance to review the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand that the location of the meeting is now different and that change is based on the documents you reviewed; however, this is not about the location. It's about who approached who when the comment was made and in what circumstances. Where in the documents that you were shown does it refresh your memory as to whether General Cermak and the group of soldiers approached you when you heard that comment, or whether it was made behind you? I -- I fail to see how, from the documents, you could derive that, so if you could explain that, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: General Cermak was in front of me; I've said as much already. And that group of people mentioned leaving the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, that was not the question. When Mr. Hedaraly put to you what you said when you were giving your statement in the district court and has pointed at some inconsistencies with what you told us today, you said, "But at the time I had not reviewed the documents." Now what Mr. Hedaraly is asking you is the following. Where in the documents do we find anything which would make it understandable that now, having reviewed the documents, you give a different version of the version you gave before the district court. Is there anything in the documents which says anything about distance, whether he approached you, what your response was. That's what Mr. Hedaraly wants to know. What in the documents explains that you gave a different version when you gave your statement before the district court, compared to your more recent version, or versions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the documents shown to me, there is nothing that specifically relates to my meeting General Cermak or how that meeting came about. But having reviewed the documents, I remembered the events, and I'm trying to explain that the meeting took place at Plavno and that I approached a group of people in the manner described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So just so I understand, you're saying that -- and we've seen that the documents that you were shown, that documents -- those -- reviewing those documents made you remember that you approach, how you approach, where the voices come from, and it all became clear to you all of a sudden. Have I understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, now, as you sit here today, you remember all of this incident very clearly, as opposed to when you gave your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Never before have I communicated with anybody concerning these events. For 15 years, that was so. So this event was forgotten. But as I was reviewing the documents, the memory came back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Including these details of who approached who, and where the voices you heard, and all of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I have 65 ter 7648, the statement to the county court, signed by the witness in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. But not -- the exhibit. Yes, this is -- will be a P exhibit then. Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2729. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2729 is admitted into evidence. Confidentiality as explained earlier. One additional question. Mr. Bilobrk, you said it was only by reading these documents that my memory came back. Why did you tell all kind of details at the time without having a memory on the matter? You gave quite some details at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave a general account. It wasn't all that detailed. It all related to more or less the same thing. In this section of the statement given to the county court in Zagreb, the proceedings did not relate to General Cermak but to other persons against whom proceedings are underway in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But facts are facts, irrespective, you as a police officer are supposed to know that. Facts are facts irrespective in what case these facts are established. Why didn't you say at the time, I just don't know; I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions, I did provide that answer, I don't remember. But let me go back to this section of the text about leaving weapons. I said to the county court that this was opinion, just like I was explaining to you this story about the weapons, only these two words were left out of my statement, the words "my opinion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you didn't -- you didn't say, This is wrong. I reviewed it. I'm not going sign because you should put it's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this statement was not given to me to read under Article 77. I only -- I heard the judge dictating the court reporter, what she should put in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are other differences. You say, I didn't go that much in details. You're giving details both today and at the time as what you responded to any suggestion of putting weapons there. Today you told us that your response was, If this is it what you mean, you should have done it earlier. But before the district court you have other details. You say: "When I heard that, I said that I was not going to place any weapons and that I do not consent to this and that if they wanted to do this, that they should have done that earlier so that I wouldn't know about it." Now, I am not going to put weapons there is different from if this is what you mean, you should have done it earlier, because this -- this suggests that part of the conversation was that you would be involved in putting the weapons there. That's what is clearly the suggestion of your statement and at least the language is different. Now, if you say, I didn't give details. It was just my opinion. I think what you responded or the gist of your response was is not primarily a matter of opinion but a matter of facts, which you either do remember or do not remember. And, therefore, it comes a bit as a -- your explanation is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that I wrongly presented the facts to the county court. I can see here, though, that the court itself wrongly presented some facts. I may have said this verbatim, but I cannot describe this statement in detail now. Or, rather, I can't explain it, because it is unclear to me even now whether I really said these words or if somebody misunderstood or misinterpreted my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at the end of this statement, it reads: "Cautioned in terms of Article 77 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, I think it is ZKP, he does not request that the record be read out as he had followed the judge's dictation out loud, and he signs it." Which, in some way, is committing yourself to the statement. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. This says that it was, indeed, like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilobrk, you were interviewed about the events on that day on a number of times previously; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I'll just, for the sake of time, run through all the interviews and ask you to confirm that you were interviewed by these people. So you were first interviewed by Mr. Franjo and some others on behalf of the Defence, one of the Defence teams for the generals; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I think it was last year, in August maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you sign a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Then you were also interviewed twice by Mr. Badzim from the MUP. The first time in the presence of a colleague of yours, Mr. Vrticevic, and a few days again later, by yourself. Do you remember those interviews?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You don't remember, or you do remember?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was just an interpretation error. And there were two Official Notes produced after these interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I think so. You showed them to me and so did the Defence, before interviewing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you were also interviewed then again by two other MUP officers, Mr. Gerovac and Mr. Mikulic in November; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then we discussed that you were interviewed also by the county court in Zagreb in February of this year, right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor in March of this year, and you signed a statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, finally, you were interviewed by the Defence team of General Cermak in April and May of this year, and you also signed a statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So by my count, that is seven interviews where you discussed the events that happened on the 27th of August, 1995. Now, can you tell us in which of these interviews did you, for the first time, talk about that suggestion that was made to leave weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I mentioned it for the first time in the statement given to Mr. Gerovac and Mr. Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you did not discuss this either in your first interview with Mr. Franjo or in any of the two further intensives with Mr. Badzim?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you explain why you had not discussed that in your prior interviews?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Because I simply answered their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So do I have to understand that Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic specifically asked you about that suggestion and that's why you mentioned it to them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Could you please show me the statement that I gave to Mr. Gerovac and Mr. Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will show it to you. But first I just want to understand your answer because your answer was why you didn't discuss it before. And you said because those questions were not asked. So I'm asking you, does that mean that if you mentioned it to Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic that would mean that they've discussed it with you? We'll go through it later, but I first want to clarify that. And that's the reason why it appeared for the first time in any of your statements?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: They were asking me questions. And if I remember that statement well, they asked me who of the high-ranking Croatian officials had ordered, or something like that, to place the weapons there. But I don't remember the exact words because it's been a long time since I read that statement or made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'll show it to you. I just want to get the right sequence first and we'll get to it very soon. But I want to first show you the Official Note you gave to Mr. Badzim, the second one, when you were by yourself. And that is 65 ter 7623. And that's an Official Note that you had reviewed previously and that was generally accurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can tell, by simply casting a glance at it, yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
