utterances.text: Now, in the last paragraph in the English, the first paragraph after your details in the Croatian, you say: "As far as the clearing of corpses in the village of Grubori is concerned, he described how General Cermak came to the stairway outside the present day Knin police station and requested an on-site investigation in Grubori. The General was accompanied by a news reporter, but he asked them to move away while he spoke to him." And it goes on. But my question for you at this stage is -- of course, we don't have the question that Mr. Badzim asked you, but this is exactly the same -- part of the same story that happened and where that comment was made. So can you tell us why you didn't include that in your answer, when you were questioned about what happened on the 27th of August and you discussed General Cermak and journalists and people approaching you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Mr. Badzim didn't ask such questions at all. This is the text that he drafted, his Official Note. But he didn't take notes while interviewing me. Probably, he drafted it based on his memory alone, this Official Note about an interview with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So are you saying that you told him about the comment made to leave weapons and he just didn't include it, or did you not mention that? Because that's what you said earlier. I'm getting a little confused.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I didn't provide that comment because he didn't ask me about that. So I never made that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you didn't think that in the context of discussing the sanitation of the bodies in Grubori such a comment being made would be relevant or important to know for a police investigator investigating what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: You're right, but when the interview began, there had been pressures after the first interview provided to Mr. Badzim, and then he said, You just answer my questions. And that's what I did. After the first interview, there were pressures, and we had to conduct a second interview. He said that I should merely answer the questions that he would put me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And -- and what were the pressures that you -- that you had after that first interview?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: After the first interview I gave to Mr. Badzim, he made a remark that I had some information that could detrimentally affect the Defence of the generals in The Hague, which I never said to him. This may have been his opinion, but I don't know why he stated that. Anyway, my chief was called up from the directorate of the police, that unless there is another interview that I gave to Mr. Badzim there would be -- that Internal Affairs would investigate and that proceedings would be launched against us and we would be suspended, unless there is another interview with Mr. Badzim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I have 65 ter 7623 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2730. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2730 is admitted into evidence. Confidentiality as set out before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And let me just show you - because you've now mentioned it - so let's -- let me show you also that first statement -- that first Official Note of interview with Mr. Badzim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 7567. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just so I want to clear about what you said earlier. What you are referring to is at the bottom of the English in page 1, the first full paragraph after the identifying information where it says that -- "After meeting some of the members of the Defence, including Mr. Franjo Djurica, Vrticevic and Bilobrk emphasised how they had given a detailed statement on the clearing of terrain in the village of Grubori and on other events from that period. They also would like to emphasise that the Defence team asked to be notified of any subsequent requests for information regarding the talk that they had." Is that what you were referring to about what was the source of the pressure that you -- that that statement is the one that triggered the pressure for you to have a second interview?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way. As for the Defence team who first interviewed me, there were no -- there was no talk about the event itself. We only spoke -- spoke about our arrival to Grubori. The Defence team showed me photographs of two dead bodies. One was burnt; and another that had an injury to the neck. We spent some ten to 15 minutes together. We didn't speak so much. They were only interested in hearing whether those people had been massacred or not. Mr. Vrticevic was not present during that interview, although Mr. Badzim mentions it here. And about the sanitation of the terrain in the village of Grubori and what is said here, that we -- that I didn't want to go into details, that is something he never heard from me. That is his opinion. That is something he stated of his own accord. I spoke very briefly with the Defence team. They didn't take notes, and I signed no statement. We mostly spoke about the dead bodies found there and their condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is it true that they asked you to be notified -- is it true that they asked to be notified of any subsequent requests for information regarding anyone talking to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. Franjo Djurica told me that. He told me that should anybody want to talk to me about that case that I should come back to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In any of your subsequent interviews that you had, did you in fact tell Mr. Franjo?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. I did not think it would be necessary for me to inform him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. If I can have 65 ter 7567 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2731. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2731 is admitted into evidence. Confidentiality as set out before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now show you, as I had -- as I'd indicated to you that I would, the statement you -- the Official Note of interview recorded by Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 7568.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And on the first page in the middle of the page in English, it says: "The above was asked if it had been suggested to him and to his colleague, Ivica Vrticevic, who was working with him as a crime technician on the humane clearing up of the dead bodies of civilians killed in the village of Grubori, by somebody from the then-senior commanding structures of the MUP ... or the Ministry of Defence, that they should have conducted an on-site investigation in the village of Grubori, but that before that they should have placed guns next to the dead bodies of civilians who had been killed in order to make it appear as if they had put up resistance to members of special police. The above stated that the day when they went to Grubori in order to carry out the humane clearing up process, some time in the morning General Cermak came in front of the Knin police administration building, escorted by a few soldiers from his security."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Turn the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "He remembers that when Cermak arrived, he was sitting on the stairs with several colleagues whose names he does not ... remember anymore, but he allows for the possibility that among them there was, on that occasion, his colleague ... Vrticevic, when Cermak came to them, he said that an on-site investigation had to be conducted in Grubori, but that before the on-site investigation guns had to be placed next to the dead bodies in order to make it appear as if the persons killed had put resistance. He remembers he got angry at Cermak's suggestion and told him he did want to know anything about it, nor did he want to participate in it." Now, Mr. Bilobrk, I understand from your testimony today that what are you saying today is that that suggestion was made by someone behind you. My question for you is: In November 2009, did you tell Croatian investigators that that suggestion, to place guns next to the bodies, had been made by General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation or any idea why that's how they recorded this?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't know. Can you see in the part of the passage where Messrs. Mikulic and Gerovac, who perused statements I provided to Mr. Badzim, where no reference to weapons is made, they came with a story prepared in advance and with questions that they prepared in advance. Upon their arrival, they put a question to me regarding the high structures of MUP and the Republic of Croatia as to who proposed -- had proposed that. In other words, before that, they already had information which was conveyed to them - I don't know where from - and that's how they came to me, directly with that question. And as for the passage at the bottom, I never stated anything of the kind before them. If I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: And if I may provide another piece of explanation with regard to my last conversation with Mr. Mikulic and Mr. Gerovac. The two gentlemen, Mr. Mikulic and Mr. Gerovac, were waiting for me one day when I came back from the field. I didn't know who they were. In any case, a colleague of mine who had called me, he called me and told me that there will be gentlemen colleagues from Zagreb waiting for me. When I saw him -- when I met up with them, they told me that they were just passing by and that they wanted to have an informal conversation with me about some details, about some things with regard to Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now when they put that question to you about the high structures of the MUP and the Ministry of Defence, do you remember what you actually answered, what you told them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I asked them where that piece of information had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: They wouldn't answer. I told them, You are asking me to tell you something that I don't know, that I don't have a clue about. You are putting a question to me, but could you please first explain where that information came from? Because I had never mentioned weapons before. There was no reference to weapons, and now you're here and the first thing you mention is weapons. Like a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you have testified today that there was, in fact, a comment made by someone about weapons being placed there, or being left there. You've testified to this. So I'm trying to understand you wanted to know the source of the information. But did you tell them what you've told us today, that there was -- that someone did in a group make a suggestion to leave weapons and how you reacted to it and how you responded and everything you've told us today. Did you tell them this?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation I provided to them was exactly the same as the one I provided here. But they did not take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: How can you have given them the same information, if part of the information that you gave us today was based on the documents that the Defence showed you that triggered your memory about all the details that that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, not in the same statement as earlier today in the court. In any case, I explained to them that there was reference made to the weapons. I explained to them that there was reference made to the weapons. But they did not embark on any details. They did not continue that conversation. They did not make any notes. They did not make any record. We were standing by the window of the building of the police administration. We lit cigarettes, and that's how we conversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you mention to them that General Cermak was -- was there as part of a group and ...

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have 65 ter 7568 in evidence. I don't know if it makes more sense to have it MFI'd for now or have it admitted right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2732. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2732 is admitted into evidence and remains confidential until further order. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me, just for the record, briefly show you the statement you gave to the -- to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which is 65 ter 7621. And if we go to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There you say: "A group of around 15 people in uniform, including who I now know to be General Cermak, came towards me. One soldier from the group asked me if we were the people doing the sanitation. I answered yes." I'll just skip the next sentence for the sake of time. "Before any conversation started between the group and me, I heard that someone from the group proposed to someone else something like: Weapons should be placed first. I don't think that [sic] comment was addressed to me but, rather, to another member of the group. It was clear to me that the suggestion I heard was to place guns next to the bodies to make it look as if they put up resistance. I immediately turned and angrily said that there would be no such placing of weapons. I added that if they wanted to do this, they would have done it before coming to me and without my knowledge. My comment stopped any further discussion of placing weapons." So I just want to -- to set out all your interviews now that we've been through almost all of them. So the first three interviews there was no mention made of any suggestion of leaving weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I see that in your official translation the word used is placing weapons; whereas, in my statement I used the verb leaving weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you for the clarification. So the first three interviews, the one with Mr. Franjo and the two, one with Mr. Badzim, there was no mention of any suggestion made; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That in the Official Note regarding the interview with Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic, that note says that General Cermak made that statement, although are you saying that that is not correct, right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then to the -- to the judge in -- in Zagreb and to the Office of the Prosecutor, we went through the one with the judge earlier, if you remember. There you say that it was made by the group that approached you, that suggestion. And now today, you're telling us that it came from behind you. Have I -- have I correctly outlined all the -- all the interviews and what you had said about that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: This definitely happened behind my back. Perhaps nobody asked for any detailed explanations. In any case, somebody in the group behind my back mentioned leaving weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just very briefly now, because I've already run out of time. I just want to very briefly go through the two other arguments you had with General Cermak that day. The one about the on-site investigation; and the one about the journalists being present when you carried out your tasks. Can you tell us where the argument about the on-site investigation took place?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: In Plavno, after my first encounter with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was it right after that -- what you discussed today, the comment was made, your reaction, was it right after?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That was after the comments and discussions about weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Cermak tell you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak asked me to carry out an inspection in Grubori, in the place where those dead bodies were found. I refused. And I explained to Mr. Cermak that I was not equipped to carry out any investigations or inspections and that there were no legal provisions in place that would make such an investigation or inspection legal, that legal conditions were not met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that line 57, 19 has word a not used by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's verify that. You said, Mr. Bilobrk: "I refused." That is, to carry out an inspection in Grubori. "And I explained to Mr. Cermak ..." What did you explain to him because it may have been mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I refused General Cermak's request to carry out an on-site investigation in Grubori. He persisted. On several occasions, he insisted that I would carry out an on-sight investigation, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just first of all seeking clarification of what you said, not a further explanation. Could it be where it was translated that you were not equipped to carry out an investigation that you were not competent to carry out an investigation; or did you say, We were not equipped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have the equipment which was necessary to carry out an on-site investigation, which meant that we did not have all the necessary equipment that would be required by a task to carry out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I apparently, on that line, did not spot what was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If could you assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The word instead of "inspection" being used at that passage was "on-site investigation," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that -- Mr. Hedaraly, any need to further clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You spoke not about an inspection but about an on-site investigation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that the line numbering is not always the same, so I was focussing on the wrong line. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You just said there, Mr. Bilobrk, in clarifying this last passage that you refused to follow General Cermak's request that he persisted on certain occasions. Can you explain to us how he persisted, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak -- I don't know how much he knew about the way an on-site investigation is carried out. That's why he persisted and on several occasions he repeated that we would doing the on-site investigation, and I explained to him that that was not possible. We were there on a special task which was humane sanitation, that we did not have the equipment required for an on-site investigation, which means that no legal requirements were in place for an on-site investigation, including the fact that an investigating judge was not informed, the prosecutor, the county prosecutor was not informed, that we did not have the professional personnel that was necessary for an on-site investigation. However, he did not understand or he seemed to not understand what I was talking about. He kept on insisting until the moment Mr. Sacic interfered and got involved in that exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Cermak angry at your refusal to carry out an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: He appeared angry. He appeared angry. I was not under the authority of the Ministry of Defence, and I believe that I was not duty-bound to carry out his orders. I had my own superiors, who were in a position to issue orders to me. And as far as Mr. Cermak is concerned, none of my superiors ever told me that I should act upon his orders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cermak tell you anything about his authority in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: He did mention that he was in Knin, that he was the main person in Knin, that they were in power in Knin. But I did not pay much heed at that. I didn't know what his tasks were, what his function in Knin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Cermak wanted to carry [sic] an on-site investigation in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, since he insisted so much on that on-site investigation, I suppose that the idea behind that was to establish properly what had happened, in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that by the 27th of August, you were already familiar with Mr. Cermak because you had seen him give statements on -- on -- in the media. By that time, were you familiar with any statements given by Mr. Cermak to the media or to the public regarding what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. I mentioned his figure from some previous appearances in the media, and those had nothing whatsoever to do with Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And then, finally, you also had another argument with General Cermak later on in Grubori regarding the presence of journalists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you -- well, first of all, how did you get to Grubori from Plavno? Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We took an asphalt road to a slope leading towards the hamlet our vehicle could not go any further and that agencies we transferred our equipment to Mr. Sacic's four-wheel drive, and we proceeded further to the point which was the last accessible, and that's where we all met, Mr. Cermak, myself, the journalist, we were there. And at that moment we went -- we proceeded with our part of the job and Mr. Cermak told us that the journalists would accompany us and that they would observe the way we worked, and that was not provided for by law. And I refused that. I did not allow the journalists to come with us. He kept on insisting on that. He wanted the journalists to come with us. Mr. Sacic again intervened, and he said that journalists could not be part of the police procedure, that a journalist could not go to the site with the police, and as a result, the journalists did not accompany us, did not come with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Cermak wanted the journalists to be present?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I suppose that Mr. Cermak, having invited the journalists, or maybe the journalists had come themselves. I don't know how they had found out about the events. That he wanted the journalists to be able to inform the public of what had happened at Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, usually I say I'm looking at the clock, but I saw that you were looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Only a few more questions, and I'll be done Your Honour. Two or three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Really, in one or two minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you went with Mr. Sacic to Grubori in his -- in his vehicle, did you have any -- any discussion with Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We spoke about my brother, who was a member of the police special unit. It was a short trip only, and Mr. Sacic asked me about my family name and, Is Frane any relative of yours. And I said, He's my brother. And he said, When you see him, give him my regards. And that was all the conversation I had in the vehicle with Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my examination. And I thank you for the extra half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One question seeking clarification. Mr. Bilobrk, earlier, Mr. Hedaraly read to you part of your statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecution, the 4th of March of this year. And then he left out one line. And then soon after that you said, "Well, the translation is -- I see that in your official translation the word used is 'placing weapons,' whereas in my statement I use the verb 'leaving weapons.'" That's the only comment I heard which came spontaneously. You were not asked about any other comments. Were there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- other matters in the portion that was read to you which you say is not consistent with what you said, what you told them during the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I signed the statement in English. The people from the OTP said that the procedure was such that a translation of the statement has yet to be -- had yet to be made. And this is the first time I had the chance to review the statement in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had a very simple question for you. My question was: You commented on that word, which, in your view, was not reflecting what you said; "leaving" instead of "putting." My simple question is: Is in any other respect what was read to you and what you apparently have had an opportunity to review yesterday, is in any other respect this text reflecting something different from what you said on the 4th of March or whether it reflects, apart from that one correction, what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this should be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For example, one of the elements I didn't find in other statements is that you were asked whether you were the people who do the sanitation. And that, for example, is -- is one of the other elements read to you. And that's what you said, on the 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I can rely on the other matters which you have not commented on, that reflects what you stated on the 4th of March of 2010.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, talking about this text, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm exclusively dealing with the portion which was read to you, and, as I understand, you had an opportunity yesterday to read in your own language. Mr. Kay, will you be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for the Prosecution [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Two words that have been used that I want to clarify with you as to their meaning. "Ostaviti," in Croatian, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: In the Croatian translation, it means leave something where it belongings, where it should be, or some similar context. This glass here has its place in a cupboard, so you're supposed to leave it in the cupboard, where it belongs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Another word: "Postaviti," with a P in front. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That word in translation should mean putting something where it doesn't belong, where it cannot usually be found, where it isn't part of a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are we talking about, then, on the 27th of August, when you were in Plavno, and you heard someone behind you mention something about weapons, either of these words, "ostaviti" or "postaviti"?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: It was "ostaviti," leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I want to ask you questions now, following up what Mr. Hedaraly was talking about, the investigating -- on-site investigation. I'd like you to see a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P503, which is under seal. Can we go to the Croatian original, page 56. And, for the English, it's the second translation of this exhibit at page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see it in a moment on your screen, Mr. Bilobrk. Second translation, page 29, and the original page, 56. Don't look at the English one but look at the Croatian. It's not up yet.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: There's a handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I can't really read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just while we're waiting for the right page to come up, can you comment whether you've ever seen this document before? Do you recognise it at all? Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the Croatian, the date is the 27th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The English text needs a correction, Your Honour, it has the 28th of August, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just go down to the fourth cross where you see the name Begonja. If that could be looked at by you. Can we have all the text, please. Thank you. If you could just read that out, as you understand that handwritten text to be, what it says.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I have difficulty reading this handwriting. It isn't easily legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let put it up for you in a bigger form. Thank you. But we've lost the bit -- there we are. Can you see where it says: Begonja. Does that make it easier for you to read that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, I can make out Prosecutor Begonja, that the team will be late, up to one hour late. Since there is a case of death, that he - he, or somebody - is engaged in an on-site investigation. That's how I interpret this section of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could confirm whether you've seen or not this document before. Have you ever seen it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't remember this document. I don't remember the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. There's no suggestion that you have seen it. I'm just confirming that matter. Just looking at that -- that entry there, though, were you aware on the 27th of August, 1995 that a public prosecutor had been contacted by the Knin duty officer to go and make an on-site investigation in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, nobody informed us of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Nothing in that document said it was Grubori, an investigation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm putting my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This has been misattributed in date in the translation, and this is a -- a pertinent matter to events on the 27th of August, which I'm entitled to ask this witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you should not suggest implicitly what it was about. You should verify with the witness whether he knows that, and we should verify that on another basis as well. Just looking at that, it should be clear what is in the text and what is not in the text, because what is in the text we could easily seek confirmation of that. What is not in the text would require a different approach to establish any of such thing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that there had been a delay in an investigating judge coming to investigate that morning, on the 27th of August? Did that message get communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that's all I ask on that matter. I want to now go through a statement that you gave to the Defence, which is a document signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have 2D00-864, please. And if the Croatian language version may be put on the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, do you identify this as a statement that you gave to the Defence and signed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the bottom of the first page? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last page, please. Do you confirm your signature on -- on that page, on the 12th of May, 2010?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the all-in-between pages are signed by the witness as well, so if I may just proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there's a written submission that the Prosecution does not oppose against admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If I could confirm the matters within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, when you gave that statement to the Defence, was everything that was stated within there, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to check that statement, to make sure that it was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers that were given in the making of -- of that statement, in court today?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might that statement be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D2048. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2048 is admitted into evidence. Confidentiality as set out before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, within that statement there are two documents that remain to be made exhibits. At paragraph 30, there is a document referred to as JB 1, a photograph, 2D00-855, might that photograph be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection. And if the second one is a second photograph, there will be no objection to that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. That's 2D00-856. May they be given exhibit numbers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, two numbers please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, first document 2D00-855 shall be assigned Exhibit D2049. Second document, 2D00-856 shall be assigned Exhibit D2050. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both admitted into evidence, confidentiality as set out before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, that's various formalities that I've done there in relation to your statement. I now want to ask you some questions. You have been referred to a large number of statements that you made before you gave this witness statement to the Defence, and you told the Court that, having seen documents, you were able to recollect better what happened on the 27th of August, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were first asked questions in 1999 by the other people who came to see you, Mr. Badzim, Mr. Gerovac -- 2009, sorry. 2009. Mr. Gerovac, Mr. Mikulic, and in 2010 the Office of the Prosecutor and also in 2009, the investigating judge. You were being asked questions of events that had happened 14 years previously. How easy was it for you to remember accurately what had happened when those bodies asked you those questions?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: It's impossible to remember some things after 14 or 15 years. That's a mighty long time. I mean, without documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the Defence came to see you in Split in this year and produced documents originating from the 27th of August, 1995, did that assist you in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What effect did looking at those documents have upon what you could recollect?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I remembered situations that I was faced with on that day, and it jogged my memory of some things that are not contained in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, the earlier statements all refer to events on the 27th of August, when you came across Mr. Cermak outside Knin police station and there was exchange of words between you and him. That description of that place and what happened and the background to that description, where did you get that from? How did that arise, that you referred to being on the steps at Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Sir, we were in front of the Knin police station daily, and we set off to the field daily from that place. It's there that we received information about such bodies. And I remember from those times that I met Mr. Cermak there, because we always left from there to go to the field. I was not aware about Strmica before that. I didn't remember any of these field missions. Everybody mentioned -- was mentioning Grubori to me, and I thought that on that day, we left to Grubori from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So is the statements that had been made earlier of any meeting between you and Mr. Cermak outside Knin police station, is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Now that I remember the details, yes, they are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what was described about what took place in the street outside Knin police station - who was there, the number of people, the scene - was that description, as well, wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Indeed. It all happened differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock and I would have let you continue for another couple of minutes if LiveNote had not collapsed and when we tried to reconnect, that's -- even the results were worse than before, so therefore I suggest that we have a break first and resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before you continue, when I said before the break, that you were counsel for the Prosecution, that was a slip of the tongue. And Freud has got nothing to do with that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, I didn't get the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now about the statement taken by Mr. Gerovac and Mr. Mikulic. And I want you to describe, first of all, how they approached you, in order to discuss with you what had happened on the 27th of August. How were you approached by them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: On that day, I was in the field. I think that I wasn't to Ploce and Makarska around 4.00 p.m. I left Makarska. A colleague phoned me and said that some colleagues from Zagreb were waiting for me, that they wanted to see me. I asked which colleagues. And he replied, well, you will see once you arrive. I expected a -- a colleague with whom I co-operated. When I arrived at the police administration, Mr. Vrticevic said that they were waiting for me upstairs at the general crime department and that they were interested in the Grubori incident. And so I went upstairs to the Department of General Crime, and the colleague took me to the office where these people were. I had known one of them by sight. There was a case of murder in our police administration and he also worked on it. I said hello, and we spoke about that incident a little. We spoke about ten minutes about that case. It was a specific case. And then he said to me that they were passing by and that they wanted to talk to me about Grubori, and I asked what -- how do you want us to talk? Formally or informally? And he said no, just like that, to see whether you remember some things. This is how we established contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it formally or informally that they were -- that they had represented to you they were going to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long did they speak to you about Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We spoke for some ten minutes or so. We little a cigarette. We opened a -- the window, and after ten minutes, we went our own separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they take any notes of that discussion at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. We were all standing. One of the colleagues was a non-smoker and the other was a smoker, but I don't really remember which one lit a cigarette with me. So we were standing by the window while we were talking about Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they say they were going to compile an Official Note of what you had discussed with them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they record the interview in any other way, with a tape recorder, for instance, or a video recorder?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I wasn't warned of that and I didn't observe any recording device. They never said that they would record anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first see their Official Note recording what was discussed between you and them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I saw it first time when you gentlemen from the Defence came to interview me, or, rather, no -- sorry. I saw it for the first time when the gentlemen from the OTP came to interview me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you keep a record of that interview after the OTP had shown it to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive any copy of the interview I gave to either Mr. Badzim or to Mr. Gerovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was your reaction when you saw the Official Note, as recorded by Gerovac and Mikulic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that I was angry. This may be the most convenient term to use now. Because they had written down things that I had never told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever said to them that General Cermak had suggested placing guns next to the dead bodies at Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. They came to me with that information. That's what they suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how did they suggest that to you? Describe what happened in the time that you spent with them. How did they suggest it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: During that conversation, or while we conversed, rather, I can't remember which one of them mentioned that first. I can't repeat the words verbatim. In any case, what they said was this. We came by information that General Cermak offered, or suggested, that you should place weapons by the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what did you say to that, when that was stated by one of them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I told them that Mr. Cermak never said that to me, and it would have been strange if a person whom I saw for the first time among a group of people to say that to me. It would have been totally strange and didn't make much sense to imagine that somebody I saw for the first time came up to me and said, Take weapons and place them by the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I wonder whether you can help us with this. An Official Note, such as this, taken by Gerovac and Mikulic, is that a document you would normally ever see?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I think that this document could have reached him through some other channels. Otherwise, I would not have seen him -- seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the procedure, is it this in Croatia, that when a Official Note is taken from a witness, he doesn't get to see the document because it's not recorded at the time, if it's not recorded at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the document, then, is made up later, several days afterwards, in the normal procedure in the Croatian investigating system, again, would that witness not be given a copy of that document and not see what was written?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any truth in the document written by him where it is stated that Cermak said that: "... an on-site investigation had to be conducted in Grubori but before that on-site investigation, guns had to be placed next to the dead bodies in order to make it appears as if the persons killed had put up resistance." Was there any truth that that was said by you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: The only truth is in the part that Mr. Cermak asked me to carry out an on-site investigation. As far as placing weapons there, before the on-site investigation started, there is not an iota of truth in that, and I never stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a policeman who investigates crimes some of the background detail, such as you were sitting on stairs with several colleagues, if you had been sitting on stairs with several colleagues, would the identities of those colleagues be discoverable even today by going to the records at Zadar-Knin police station, police administration?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: One might do that. Because those men were employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Defence, you refer to civilian protection officers also involved on the 27th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are those the sorts of colleagues, if you had been sitting on the stairs waiting for a job at Knin police station, are those the sort of colleagues who could have been questioned to find out if what you said was true, if you said it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how many civilian protection officers did you work with?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I believe that there were four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many fire officers did you work with? Explosives officers.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: There were no fire officers involved. There were only two or three explosives officers. It depended on the mission. There were some situations when only two were sent; and if they were not too busy, then sometimes even three or four would accompany us on on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So to find out if you were telling the truth, would you agree, others could have been questioned to find out if this story is true?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the investigating judge at the county court in Zagreb spoke to you in 2010, did you just give him an account that we see on this page and which you looked at this morning with Mr. Hedaraly? Did you just state this as an entire statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I explained to the judge about an event, and then the judge dictated to the secretary and the secretary recorded my statement. In this part of the statement, as I've already stated in answering the Prosecutor's questions, two words were left out from what I said, from what I opined. I said that two words were missing from the statement, as it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some questions about the taking of this statement in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, since the e-court system is causing a lot of problems, could you remind me of the exhibit number which was assigned to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have looked it up under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 2729, the judge's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The record of interview to the county court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend. My LiveNote's gone down here, but I will remind myself again as to what I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was -- I'm going to ask you about how this statement was taken in Zagreb which was compiled on 16th of February, 2010. How long were you questioned for in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I believe that the whole interview lasted for some 15 or 20 minutes. But I can't be sure of that, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've just seen on the document it commenced at 12.05 and it completed at 12.50. How long did it take to write the statement during that 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That's the total time. I first provided my statement to the judge, explaining what happened. Then the judge would dictate that part to the secretary, and then the secretary would record what the judge was dictating to her. That's how the interview proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, if I can ask you this: Did the judge in Zagreb, does he have a copy of the Official Notes taken by the police officers?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I don't know. I was never shown any Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I know you weren't shown, but it's just a procedural matter, whether you know for a fact, as a policeman, whether the investigating judge has information that -- that you don't have or -- but he has a file with it in.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: As a rule, he should have had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, this statement is set in Knin, where you are alleged to have spoken to General Cermak. Did you have any access to any sort of documents to refresh your memory as to what was said or what happened at that time for these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is recorded as you having said that you were approached by General Cermak and a group of soldiers surrounding him. Now, in all that took place, when you saw General Cermak on the 27th of August, was he ever surrounded by a group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: General Cermak was, indeed, with a group of soldiers. We were all within that group. There were journalists. All of us were there in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The word I'm interested in is "surrounding him." So that he's in a middle of a group, that he's surrounded by a group. Was that ever a picture that happened on the 27th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but if -- maybe it would be, if we're going to quote from the document, I think it's not "surrounded," now it's "around." Surrounding was before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any dispute about what was said, then a literal quote is to be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'll ask him to do it -- well, it may be that I've got an earlier version of a translation here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd read it literally --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you have in your version --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then if Mr. Hedaraly has newer one than you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if Mr. Hedaraly could read it out that would indeed assist me, as I think I've got an earlier version, then, of the translation, if it's been updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's just that there's two mentions. There's the group surrounding General Cermak and then later on the group around him approached me. I just don't know which quote that Mr. Kay was referring to. Maybe it's just to put it on the screen, it could just be much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I'll just stay with my original question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he ever surrounded, in the understanding of that word, by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Not surrounded in the classical sense of that word, but he was within the group, among -- among soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what I would like to go to now is the questions that you were asked by the Office of the Prosecutor, when they interviewed you. Did you ever tell them that General Cermak never mentioned anything about placing guns or leaving guns or putting guns?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. I said that on no occasion had General Cermak referred to either leaving or placing weapons by the dead bodies. General Cermak spoke to me only on one occasion and on that occasion he mentioned the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go to Plavno. And you said that you arrived there from Strmica. How many vehicles travelled from Strmica to Plavno?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I believe that there were three. The civilian protection in their own vehicle; we in our own vehicle, myself and my colleague, Vrticevic; and explosives experts travelled in their own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at that photograph, JB/1, that you produced in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 2049.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you could just look at that photograph. This is identified in your statement as being the place near a creek or bridge where cars had stopped. Are you able to describe to us where your vehicles parked, having travelled from Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: We were supposed to be even further behind these vehicles, and you can't see them in this part of the photo. I remember this well. This is a very short section and there were quite a few vehicles double-parked on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have facilities where you can mark on -- on the screen for us, if that will assist the Court. Firstly, how many vehicles were parked here. You've just indicated on the screen -- if you could indicate on the screen where your vehicle stopped?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Our vehicle should be somewhere here, behind this part at the very far end of the photo, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how wide is this road?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: About 3 metres wide. Actually, it is a village road and village roads are normally 3 metres wide, although it is a double circulation road. The traffic goes in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many vehicles were stopped at this place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to -- if we could just get information from Mr. Kay whether this is a recent photograph or a contemporaneous photograph, whether -- you know, was it shown to the witness before -- I mean, just to have some background on the photograph just so we know what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a recent photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there anything about this photograph that is different from the 27th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: It was not as green as I can see it in this photo. In any case, I recognise this little bridge in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: And there was a dry creek here, where we found a skeleton while we were standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how many cars had stopped here in this place?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know how many. Probably a dozen or so. There were journalists, there were our three vehicles, the army vehicles, the special police vehicles. I'm sure that there were around ten or so vehicle there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And whereabouts were -- were those vehicles parked?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: All the vehicles pulled over on the road in this part, and that's where they were all parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were people just standing around generally in this area, as a -- as a random group of people?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Most of the group were here by the bridge, in this part here. And that's where we met up with General Cermak as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said you saw General Cermak with journalists.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were those journalists and he?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: If my memory serves me properly, in this part here. The vehicles were parked by this side, and in this part here, there was a larger group of people. General Cermak was somewhere around here, in front of us, with a group of journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described hearing someone behind you saying about leaving the weapons, or putting the weapons. Whereabouts did that statement come from? Are you able to mark on this photograph for us?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: When we joined that group of people, and I don't know whether it was in this part exactly or maybe a couple of metres further. In any case, behind me while we were all talking, behind me I heard a voice referring to the leaving of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just mark the general whereabouts of where that was said with -- with an X for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Well, if I was here, then that voice came from somewhere around here, from that part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just mark for me a square where you were, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you could mark for me a C, where Mr. Cermak was, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Here, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were there people standing in between you and Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: The vehicles were parked here. We met up here on this side of the road. We could not gather around the vehicles. That was the group of people, there, in this part. We were standing in -- in a line, not exactly in a very neat line like troops would be in a lineup, but we were standing in a sort of a -- a line. We were not in a circle. We were not just randomly standing there. We were kind of lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But so we get this clear, at that time when a remark is made about leaving weapons, were a number of people chatting, talking in a random fashion?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. People were talking or -- they were conversing. There were groups of two or three talking amongst each other. People all -- everybody was saying something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so the 30 or so people that you stated in your statement, were they in this general area that you've marked out on the photograph at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I know Mr. Kay mentioned 30 people. I think that may be in the statement, but I think today the witness stated an approximate number that was much less and it seems that that's what we should go with if we ask questions to him not based on some earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it should be clear what we're doing, whether you try to refer to the one or to the other version is -- but it should be clear. Mr. Kay, apart from that, you referred to the marking. To say that without a further description on the record that it would be immediately clear to everyone what we referred to, is, on the basis of the markings, not very clear. But I do understand that the marking on the far right is where the witness's car was. That what is -- seems to an interrupted horizontal line is a dry creek where two lines at where there are some small poles is said to be a bridge. And that where the people gathered or where they were seems to be on the part of the road marked which goes from left under to a bit more right up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so that it's clear, how many people were at this location when you heard the remark that we've been discussing? How many people?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I heard the Prosecutor's -- the Prosecutor's remark about some 15 to 20 or maybe there were -- and you were saying about 30 or so. I can try and clarify, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Forget what we've said. You just tell us what you say is the number of people who were here at this location at that time when you heard this remark.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Here, in this area, there were some 20 people or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by "this area," so that it's clear to us, could you mark a line across this picture, when you say "this area, about 20 people." Can you mark where --

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Here, in this area, where there was large group of people, well, they were about 20 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we have the traditional problem that marking in colours means something. This red marking is done at the request of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that it needs to be corrected. It is now on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I was going describe it as being a red mark now on the photograph. Don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then the number of people entirely in this location, is that a different number?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. We found a group of some 15 to 20 people there, and seven or eight of us joined them. So that would make a total of about 30 people, once we had joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so it's clear, you're being asked what Mr. Cermak could have heard on your description of the events, is it right that Mr. Cermak was on the other side of you to where the remark was made.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You are being asked to say whether he could have heard that remark. Now, based upon everything you've told us - the number of people, where Mr. Cermak was, where you were, where the person who made the remark, given the scene that was happening - can you say if Mr. Cermak heard that remark?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether he heard it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking -- looking back now and having looked and analysed this 15 years later, do you agree that it's highly unlikely, given those circumstances, that he could have heard the remark to which you reacted?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Given the distance between him and me, he might have heard it. But, of course, I don't know whether he was in another conversation or whether he was focussed on other conversations around him, whether he was paying attention. That's something I cannot comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So let us now look at that remark that he might have heard and to which you reacted. If you could just repeat to the Court the words that you heard.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: First, weapons should be left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know who said that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. Somebody behind my back said those words. I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if that person was speaking to anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: When I turned around and made my comment, I couldn't identify the person who had said that. I couldn't tell. But they were talking to each other, so who said those words to who, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you reacted, did anyone reply to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone respond in any physical way to what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. They continued talking as if nothing had happened. In fact, I don't know what that -- what they were referring to, or they may have -- they may not have heard my remark that I uttered when I turned around and faced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask that you, whether you know if anyone heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. I don't know, because nobody reacted to my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know -- you don't know whether, in fact, the context of what you heard was connected with how you reacted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked questions earlier this morning about what you understood. Would you agree with me, having looked at this evidence, that you were not in a position to be sure about the context of this remark?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when you were asked what you understood it to mean, you don't know what the maker of the statement or remark was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is it right that no weapons were placed next to bodies when you went to Grubori to perform your tasks?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: That is right. And the photographs that we took and the video footage we made shows that, indeed, no weapons were placed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So other than that moment here, did anyone at any other time on that afternoon suggest that you, in some way, fabricate the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. It is my duty as a forensic technician to preserve the crime scene the way it was when I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, were any of your colleagues who you were working with on that day requested to manufacture a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. My colleagues, to the extent I know them, would not agree to that. They would -- they wouldn't do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And -- and this remark you heard and your reaction, did you report it to anyone that day as being a matter that should be investigated?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, I didn't consider it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or at any other stage in the subsequent weeks or months, did you report it to anyone so that they could investigate it to discover the significance?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you, once we arrived at Grubori, I interpreted this leaving of weapons differently, that word. Because we all had long-barrelled weapons. We entered the village with only personal weapons on us, me and my colleagues anyway. The reason was that there was still some people alive there. A crime had been committed, and a group of people armed with long-barrelled and short-barrelled weapons was entering the village again, and I interpreted this leaving of weapons the way I did. And then it completely slipped my memory, and I considered it unnecessary to report anything to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So looking back at it now - because it's your reaction that people are analysing about this - would you agree that you could have misinterpreted that remark at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was nothing else happening on that day that -- that involved falsifying the crime scene with weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No, nothing else happened. We did our job the usual way as on any other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The sort of people in that area who were standing around there, can you recollect what types of people they were, where they came from, if they were official people or civilians? Can you recollect the type of people who were there in that general area?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: There was soldiers, there were members of the special police force, then me and my colleague, Mr. Vrticevic. There were journalists. And there were several protection people; they were also civilians. And there were also bomb techs, but they were also with the civil protection. So it was a mixed group of civilians, soldiers, police and journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking back at all this, then, Mr. Bilobrk, and the numbers of statements that you've given, whom you've spoken to, and then, more latterly, to the Defence, people when they've been speaking to you about this, have any of them being trying to get you to say something that you didn't want to say? Have they -- have people at all tried to put words into your mouth, force you into a position to say something about this for them to hold a position?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, my colleagues Mr. Mikulic and Mr. Gerovac after those questions they put it me, we have mentioned their statement, who -- who -- or, rather, which high-ranking official had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat these last two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat the last few sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In replying to this question put to me by the Defence, Mr. Gerovac and Mr. Mikulic, who had interviewed me, came with this information and their first question was who -- or, rather, which high-ranking official had told me to put weapons beside the dead bodies. And in -- that's what they mentioned in this statement, and they meant Mr. Cermak, because they mentioned his name in their question, General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you were seen by the Defence and interviewed and shown documents that form the basis of the statement that's an exhibit, did the Defence try and put any words into your mouth, get you to say something you didn't want to say, make suggestions to you, turn your words around in any way when you made your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And -- and were you given as long as you like to look at the documents, your previous statements, the record of your interview with the Defence in your own language, without any pressure and free to speak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you used the words as "long as you like," "without any pressure." I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I do anything else, can I make the photograph with the markings an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the marked photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit D2051. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We can admit it into evidence. I'm not sure how helpful it is, but there are some indications so that we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to do my utmost best [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I found it very helpful for my part, Your Honour, if Mr. Hedaraly is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's in evidence and let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we'll have to conclude for the day. Could you give us an indication as to where you are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just review notes overnight I will not be very long. I've got a feeling here, but I'd like to talk to those I work with just to see if I should have covered something today. I tried to keep it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either nothing or as relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it will be relatively short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd say about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About half an hour. Which means that most likely we'll conclude - I'm also looking at you, Mr. Hedaraly - during the first session tomorrow morning. Then before we continue, let me first instruct the witness. Mr. Bilobrk, we'll adjourn for the day. We'll start again tomorrow morning at 9.00. You should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way with anyone, whomever that is, about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today, or testimony still to be given tomorrow. So total silence in your communication with others. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the usher escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For tomorrow, the proposed schedule is the following. From 9.00 to 10.45 first session; then a short break, 11.10 until 1.00, second session; from 2.00 to quarter to 4.00, third session. From ten minutes past 4.00 until 5.30 the fourth session. And, if need be, the last fifth session between 6.00 p.m. and 7.00 p.m. That will be our schedule for tomorrow. We'll adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 3rd of June, 9.00 in this same Courtroom III. But perhaps we should have returned to open session -- but -- perhaps that's better to do that, so that I apologise for the inconvenience, everyone rising. Mr. Registrar, could we just return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, the 3rd of June, 9.00 in the morning, but will turn into private session immediately and most likely for the remainder of that day. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
